authoredSolutions.1: Each of the four columns carries a quarter of the load. \[F = \frac{Mg}{4} = \frac{50 \times 10^{3} \times 9.8}{4} = 1.225 \times 10^{5}\text{ N}\] The load-bearing cross-section is an annulus of outer radius \(1.00\text{ m}\) and inner radius \(0.50\text{ m}\): \[A = \pi\left( R^{2} - r^{2} \right) = \pi\left( 1.00^{2} - 0.50^{2} \right) = 0.75\pi = 2.356\text{ m}^{2}\] \[\text{strain} = \frac{\text{stress}}{Y} = \frac{F}{AY} = \frac{1.225 \times 10^{5}}{2.356 \times 2.0 \times 10^{11}} = 2.60 \times 10^{- 7}\]
authoredSolutions.2: For an equilateral triangle of side \(a\), the perpendicular distance from the centroid to each side is \[r = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{3}} = \frac{0.09}{2\sqrt{3}} = 0.02598\text{ m}\] Each side is a finite straight conductor subtending \(60^{\circ}\) on either side of the foot of the perpendicular, so it contributes \[B_{1} = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r}\left( \sin 60^{\circ} + \sin 60^{\circ} \right) = \frac{10^{- 7} \times 1.5}{0.02598} \times \sqrt{3} = 1.0 \times 10^{- 5}\text{ T}\] All three sides give fields in the same sense, so \[B = 3B_{1} = 3 \times 10^{- 5}\text{ T}\] With the current flowing clockwise, the right-hand rule puts the field into the plane of the triangle.
authoredSolutions.3: Each sphere contributes its own moment of inertia about its centre plus a parallel-axis term. authoredSolutions.31: Read each Newman projection: I has the two methyls \(180^{\circ}\) apart in a staggered arrangement (anti, the energy minimum); III is staggered with the methyls only \(60^{\circ}\) apart (gauche, raised about \(3.8\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\) by steric strain); IV is eclipsed with each methyl eclipsing a hydrogen (partially eclipsed, about \(16\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)); II is eclipsed with the two methyls superimposed (fully eclipsed, the maximum at roughly \(19-25\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)). Increasing potential energy is therefore anti \(<\) gauche \(<\) methyl-hydrogen eclipsed \(<\) methyl-methyl eclipsed, i.e. I \(<\) III \(<\) IV \(<\) II. The correct option is (D).
authoredSolutions.32: Europium has \(Z = 63\), so neutral Eu is \([Xe]4f^{7}6s^{2}\). Removing the two \(6s\) electrons gives \(Eu^{2+} = [Xe]4f^{7}\), an exactly half-filled \(f\) subshell that would normally be expected to confer extra stability. The point of the question is that \(Eu^{2+}\) is a strong reducing agent in spite of this, because \(+3\) is the characteristic and thermodynamically favoured oxidation state of the lanthanoids, so the ion readily gives up a further electron. The outermost ground-state configuration asked for is \(4f^{7}\), option (C).
